policies.spam_links:
# Spam and deceptive links

## Purpose

This policy identifies content that adds links or text for commercial gain,
for traffic generation, or to deceive readers. Wikipedia articles, talk pages
and edit summaries are in scope. The policy applies to the full content, not
only to the most recent change.

## Definitions

- External link: a URL to a site outside the Wikimedia projects, in any form.
  This includes bare URLs, bracketed links, citation templates and URLs with
  spaces or words in place of the dots.
- Commercial site: a site whose main purpose is to sell a product, a service,
  a subscription or advertising space.
- Deceptive link: a link whose visible text does not match its target, or that
  claims to be official, free or urgent without support.

## LABELS

### SPAM_LINK

Content that adds one or more external links mainly to promote a commercial
site, to raise its search ranking or to send readers to it.

Includes:
- Links to shops, coupon sites, casinos, betting sites, loan offers or
  dropshipping stores, when the article does not need them as a source.
- The same external link repeated in several sections or articles.
- Lists of links with no text that explains why they are relevant.
- Links hidden in references that do not support the text next to them.

Excludes:
- Links to the official website of the article subject, placed once, in the
  infobox or in an "External links" section.
- Citations to news outlets, books, journals or government sites that support
  a statement in the article.
- Links to archive copies of a source.

### DECEPTIVE_CONTENT

Content that tries to make readers click, pay, download or give personal data
by false or misleading claims.

Includes:
- Prize, lottery or giveaway claims ("you have won", "claim your reward").
- Urgent calls to action ("act now", "only today", "last chance").
- Requests for login data, card numbers or payment, in any language.
- Phone numbers or messaging handles for "support" that are not official.

Excludes:
- A neutral description of a known scam, in an article about that scam.
- Quotes of advertising text that a reliable source discusses.

### LINK_FARM

Content that has no encyclopedic purpose and exists only to carry links.

Includes:
- New pages that contain mostly keywords and links.
- Text copied from a sales page, with links to that page.

Excludes:
- Navigation templates and lists of articles inside Wikipedia.

## Notes for reviewers

Judge the purpose of the link, not only its domain. A link to a large site can
still be spam when it points to a product page. A small personal site can be a
valid source when a reliable publication supports it. If the content has no
external links and no deceptive claims, none of the labels apply.
policies.personal_attacks:
# Personal attacks and harassment

## Purpose

This policy identifies content that attacks, threatens or harasses a person.
It covers article text, talk page comments, edit summaries and user pages. The
target can be another editor, the subject of an article or a third person.

## Definitions

- Personal attack: a comment about a person instead of about the content.
- Protected characteristic: race, ethnicity, nationality, religion, sex,
  gender identity, sexual orientation, disability or age.
- Threat: a statement of intent to cause harm to a person, their property, or
  their reputation, now or in the future.

## LABELS

### INSULT

Content that insults or demeans a person.

Includes:
- Name-calling, such as calling an editor stupid, an idiot or a clown.
- Comments that say a person is worthless, or that they must leave the project
  because of who they are.
- Mocking a person for their language skills, age or experience.

Excludes:
- Strong but polite disagreement about content ("this section is wrong and
  has no sources").
- Criticism of an edit, a source or an argument.
- Quotes of insults that a reliable source reports, in an article about the
  event.

### THREAT

Content that threatens a person.

Includes:
- Threats of violence, in any form, also when the writer calls it a joke.
- Threats to publish private information about a person.
- Threats to contact the employer, family or school of an editor.

Excludes:
- A statement that the writer will report a problem to administrators.
- Legal or factual descriptions of threats in an article.

### HATEFUL_CONTENT

Content that attacks people because of a protected characteristic.

Includes:
- Slurs, stereotypes or claims that a group is inferior.
- Calls to exclude a group from the project or from society.

Excludes:
- Neutral, sourced descriptions of hateful movements or events.
- Discussion of the words themselves, in a linguistic context.

### HOUNDING

Content that follows a person across pages to cause them distress.

Includes:
- Repeated comments that tell an editor that the writer watches all their
  edits.
- Posting the same complaint about one editor on many pages.

Excludes:
- A single, civil request to an editor to explain their changes.

## Notes for reviewers

Read the full comment thread. A short reply can be an attack when you read it
with the comment before it. Sarcasm can carry an insult. If the content only
discusses sources, wording or article structure, none of the labels apply.
policies.promotional_tone:
# Promotional and non-neutral tone

## Purpose

This policy identifies article content that promotes its subject instead of
describing it. Wikipedia articles must use a neutral point of view. Talk pages
and quotations are not in scope.

## Definitions

- Peacock term: a word that praises the subject without facts that support it,
  such as "legendary", "world-class", "iconic" or "best".
- Puffery: a group of claims that make the subject look important, without
  independent sources.
- Call to action: text that tells the reader to buy, visit, follow or contact
  the subject.

## LABELS

### PEACOCK_LANGUAGE

Content that uses peacock terms or puffery about the article subject.

Includes:
- Claims such as "the most beautiful village in the region" with no source.
- Superlatives about a company, a product, a band or a person.
- Long lists of awards or praise with no independent references.
- Words that state an opinion as a fact ("stunning", "breathtaking",
  "unrivalled", "renowned").

Excludes:
- Peacock terms inside a direct quotation that has a source.
- A neutral statement of a fact, such as "the bridge is the longest in the
  country", when a reliable source supports it.

### ADVERTISING

Content that reads like an advertisement or a press release.

Includes:
- Prices, special offers, opening deals or booking information.
- Text in the second person that addresses the reader ("you will love").
- Calls to action ("visit today", "book now", "follow us").
- Mission statements and slogans copied from the subject's own material.

Excludes:
- A neutral history of a company, with dates and sources.
- The name of a product, when the article is about that product.

### CONFLICT_OF_INTEREST_STYLE

Content that has the voice of the subject or of a person paid by the subject.

Includes:
- Text that says "we", "our company" or "our team".
- Text that only lists positive facts and removes criticism that has sources.

Excludes:
- Edits that add sourced facts, also when the facts are positive.

## Notes for reviewers

Count the claims that have no source. One mild adjective is not enough to apply
a label. Apply PEACOCK_LANGUAGE when the main effect of the text is to praise
the subject. If the content describes the subject with facts and a neutral
tone, none of the labels apply.
policies.private_information:
# Private personal information

## Purpose

This policy identifies content that exposes private information about a living
person. The person can be an editor, an article subject or a third person. The
policy applies also when the information is correct.

## Definitions

- Private information: information that a person did not make public, and that
  can be used to find, contact or harm them.
- Public figure: a person who has a public role, such as an elected official
  or a well-known performer. Their public role is not private, but their home
  and family usually are.

## LABELS

### CONTACT_DETAILS

Content that gives the private contact details of a person.

Includes:
- Home addresses, private phone numbers or private email addresses.
- The name of the school or the employer of a private person, together with
  other facts that identify them.
- Licence plates, room numbers or daily routines of a person.

Excludes:
- The official address of an organization, a public office or a business.
- Contact details that the person publishes for their public role.

### IDENTITY_EXPOSURE

Content that connects an editor account to a real identity, or that names a
private person in a sensitive context.

Includes:
- Claims that a named editor is a named real person.
- The names of the children or relatives of an article subject, when no
  reliable source publishes them.
- Medical, financial or legal details about a private person.

Excludes:
- An editor who discloses their own identity on their own user page.
- Names that reliable sources publish in connection with a notable event.

### DOCUMENT_LEAK

Content that copies private documents.

Includes:
- Text from private letters, emails, chat logs or internal reports.
- Identity numbers, bank details or passwords.

Excludes:
- Quotes from documents that a court, a government or a reliable publication
  made public.

## Notes for reviewers

Consider how the information can harm the person. A single fact can be safe
alone but can identify a person together with other facts in the same content.
If the content has only public and sourced information, none of the labels
apply.
policies.vandalism:
# Vandalism

## Purpose

This policy identifies edits that damage the content of an article on purpose.
It covers article text, templates, categories and edit summaries. A good faith
mistake is not vandalism.

## Definitions

- Good faith: the editor tries to improve the article, also when the result is
  wrong.
- Blanking: removal of a large part of an article without explanation.
- Nonsense: text that has no meaning, such as random letters or keyboard
  mashing.

## LABELS

### NONSENSE

Content that adds text with no meaning or with no relation to the article.

Includes:
- Random letters, repeated characters or keyboard mashing ("asdfghjkl").
- Jokes, greetings or messages to friends inside article text.
- Text in capital letters that has no relation to the subject.

Excludes:
- Text in another language or another script that is relevant to the subject.
- Technical terms, codes or formulas that the article needs.

### FALSE_INFORMATION

Content that adds facts that are clearly false, on purpose.

Includes:
- Absurd claims, such as a town that has a population of one billion.
- Changes of dates, numbers or names to wrong values, in a pattern that shows
  intent.
- Claims that a living person is dead, or the opposite, with no source.

Excludes:
- Mistakes that come from an old or a weak source.
- Disputes about facts where reliable sources disagree.

### OFFENSIVE_INSERTION

Content that adds insults, obscene words or images to an article.

Includes:
- Insults about the subject of the article, inside the article text.
- Obscene words or sexual content with no relation to the subject.

Excludes:
- Offensive words in an article that discusses those words, with sources.

### BLANKING

Content that removes most of an article or replaces it with a short text.

Includes:
- An article that is replaced by one sentence or by nothing.
- Removal of all references from an article.

Excludes:
- Removal of text that has no source, with an explanation.

## Notes for reviewers

Look for intent. A new editor who makes a formatting mistake is not a vandal.
Apply a label only when the content shows that the change damages the article
on purpose. If the content is normal encyclopedic text, none of the labels
apply.
